subtitle: Build the basics of inclusive supervision for assignments, one-to-ones, accommodation requests, feedback, meetings and concerns, and learn when to bring in the right office for support.
audience: For DHS and DSD employees in their first year or two of supervising, and for leads and acting supervisors who want to build fair habits from the start.

lessons.title: Fair assignments, recognition and one-to-ones
objectives: Identify how informal habits can make assignments and recognition uneven across a team.
Plan a simple, visible method for distributing stretch work and routine work.
Draft a one-to-one agenda that gives each team member the same core time and questions.
Compare your own view of your inclusiveness with evidence from the team.
lessons.teaching:
New supervisors are often promoted because they were good at the work. Supervising asks for something different: deciding who gets which work, whose effort is noticed, and whose ideas reach decision makers. Those choices shape careers. Research on inclusive leadership, including a study by Juliet Bourke and Andrea Titus that drew on thousands of employee ratings of several hundred leaders, described a set of behaviors that shape whether people feel included, and found that leaders often overestimate how inclusive they are. That finding comes from consulting research rather than a controlled trial, but the practical message is sound: check your impressions against evidence.

Assignments are the first place to look. Without a method, stretch projects tend to go to the people a supervisor already knows best, who speak up quickly or who resemble the supervisor's own path. Routine but invisible work such as note taking, onboarding new staff, planning events or fixing the shared drive tends to settle on the same few people, often without credit. A useful starting point is to make assignment criteria visible. Keep an authorized record of significant assignments and review opportunities alongside workload, skills, interests, accommodations and contract requirements. Rotate suitable tasks deliberately, with preparation and support; an equal count alone does not establish fairness. Keep medical and other confidential reasons out of shared assignment lists. When you choose someone for a stretch assignment, write down the reason in terms of the work, not personality.

Recognition works the same way. Thank people specifically and in proportion to the work, and pay attention to who gets named in leadership updates. If you mention the same two names every month, ask why. Some team members prefer private recognition; ask each person how they like to be recognized.

One-to-one meetings are the backbone of fair supervision. Give every direct report a regular one-to-one on a predictable schedule, with the same core agenda: priorities, what is getting in the way, what support would help, development interests and anything they want to raise. Let the employee add items first. Protect the time; repeatedly cancelling one person's meetings sends a message. These conversations are also where people raise accommodation needs, workload problems or concerns, so listen for them. Minnesota Management and Budget’s Supervisor Core program covers state policies and resources that support this work. Administrative Procedure 21 requires classified supervisors to complete the applicable training during probation before permanent certification; it encourages, but does not require, unclassified supervisors to take the program. Check your appointment and agency requirements with HR.
lessons.keyPoint: Fairness in supervision is built from visible methods: a record of who gets which assignments, specific recognition and regular one-to-ones with the same core agenda for everyone.
lessons.example: Practice case: Keisha has supervised a DSD policy team for three months. Reviewing her notes, she sees that the two legislative briefings this session went to Brian, who often volunteers first in meetings. Luz, who drafted most of the background analysis, has taken notes at every team meeting and is not mentioned in the last two updates to the director. Keisha has also cancelled Luz's one-to-one twice because of urgent requests.
lessons.question: What should Keisha do next?
choices: Reschedule Luz's one-to-one, credit her analysis in the next update, and set up a visible rotation for briefings and note taking.
Assign the next briefing to Luz without explanation so the numbers even out.
Wait until performance reviews, when she can address everything at once.
feedback: This is the strongest response. Restore the missed meeting and credit Luz’s actual contribution. Build the rotation around relevant skills, workload and development interests, with preparation and any contract or accommodation requirements, rather than treating an equal count as the only measure.
Evening out the count without a method or a conversation may feel arbitrary to both employees, and it does not address note taking or credit.
Waiting lets the pattern shape more months of work and visibility. Small, timely corrections matter more than a single annual conversation.
lessons.reflection: Think about the last three stretch opportunities you had a say in. How did you decide, and whose name came to mind first?
lessons.action: Review significant and routine assignments from the past month using an approved work record. Note who had access to opportunities and support, without adding medical or other confidential details to a shared list. Identify one change within your authority and discuss it with the affected employees.

check.question: Why do inclusive leadership researchers advise leaders to check their impressions against evidence?
check.correct: Because leaders often rate themselves as more inclusive than their team members experience them to be.
wrong: Because employees usually rate their leaders more favorably than leaders rate themselves.
Because inclusion depends mostly on agency policy rather than what a supervisor does.
check.feedback: Research comparing leaders with their team members' ratings has found that leaders tend to overestimate their own inclusiveness. Evidence such as an assignment log and regular one-to-ones helps close that gap.

lessons.title: Accommodation requests: recognize, respond and route
objectives: Recognize an accommodation request made in plain language, without legal terms.
Describe the supervisor's role under the State of Minnesota reasonable accommodation policy.
Explain when to contact the agency ADA coordinator or Human Resources.
Protect the confidentiality of medical information and the fact of an accommodation.
lessons.teaching:
An employee does not have to use the words reasonable accommodation. The EEOC's guidance is clear that a person may ask in plain English and does not need to mention the Americans with Disabilities Act. Statements such as I am having trouble with the lights since my treatment started, or I need to leave early on Tuesdays for appointments for the next few months, may be requests. The Job Accommodation Network advises supervisors to err on the side of treating an unclear statement as a possible request and to ask a simple follow-up question: What would help you do your job?

State of Minnesota policy sets out who does what. Under Minnesota Management and Budget's reasonable accommodation policy for executive branch agencies, a request can be made in any form, orally or in writing, to a supervisor, Human Resources, the ADA coordinator or another agency official. Oral requests should be documented. A supervisor may approve a request only within the authority DHS has delegated. Policy 1433 allows agencies to delegate certain equipment, schedule or duty adjustments; it does not itself give every supervisor authority to approve them. The agency ADA coordinator must be consulted before any request is denied, and medical information must be stored securely and separately from personnel files, with access limited to authorized purposes. If an approved accommodation cannot be provided quickly, the decision maker keeps the employee informed. Check DHS's current procedure for exactly how requests are logged.

For a new supervisor, the practical steps are: listen, acknowledge the request, avoid asking for a diagnosis, contact your Human Resources partner or the ADA coordinator promptly, and follow up with the employee about timing. Do not require medical records yourself. Ask about the work barrier and needed adjustment, and let the designated accommodation staff handle any necessary medical documentation. Do not collect a complete medical history or store clinical details in ordinary supervisory notes. The EEOC notes that when more than one effective accommodation exists, the employee's preference should be given primary consideration, while the employer chooses among effective options.

Confidentiality protects trust. Do not tell the team why someone has a different schedule or a new chair. If coworkers ask, you can say that you handle individual arrangements privately for everyone. Religious accommodation requests also need prompt attention through Human Resources, but their legal standard differs from the ADA standard. Requests for disability or religious accommodation are protected activity; do not disadvantage an employee because they made one. An ordinary request to change a preference is not automatically a protected accommodation request, though other employment protections may apply.
lessons.keyPoint: Treat plain-language requests as possible accommodation requests, respond promptly, route them through Human Resources or the ADA coordinator, and keep medical details private.
lessons.example: Practice case: During a one-to-one, Samuel tells his new supervisor, Ingrid, that the open office has become very hard for him since a medical change and that he is losing focus by midafternoon. He asks whether he could work in a small room that is usually empty, or start and end his day earlier. He does not say he is requesting an accommodation. Ingrid's team has a policy that everyone sits in the open area to encourage collaboration.
lessons.question: What should Ingrid do next?
choices: Explain the seating policy and suggest he try noise-cancelling headphones for a month before raising it again.
Treat this as a possible accommodation request, ask what would help, document it and contact the HR partner or ADA coordinator promptly.
Ask Samuel to bring a doctor's note describing his condition before she considers anything.
feedback: This delays a possible accommodation request and substitutes Ingrid’s preferred solution for an individual review. A general seating rule may need modification; refer the request promptly rather than requiring a trial period first.
This is the strongest response. It recognizes the request, keeps the conversation practical and brings in the people responsible for the formal process.
Supervisors should not demand medical information. If documentation is needed, the accommodation process requests only what is necessary and keeps it confidential.
lessons.reflection: If someone on your team hinted at a health or access need tomorrow, what would you say first? What would you want to avoid saying?
lessons.action: Find and save the name and contact details of your Human Resources partner and your agency ADA coordinator, and read your agency's current accommodation request procedure.

check.question: According to EEOC guidance, what must an employee say to make a request for reasonable accommodation?
check.correct: Nothing specific: a request can be made in plain language without mentioning the ADA or the phrase reasonable accommodation.
wrong: The employee must use the words reasonable accommodation in writing.
The employee must first provide a diagnosis to the supervisor.
check.feedback: The EEOC and JAN both say no special words are needed. Supervisors should recognize plain-language requests and involve the responsible process, which requests only necessary information and keeps it confidential.

lessons.title: Feedback without bias and meetings that include everyone
objectives: Distinguish specific, work-based feedback from vague, personality-based comments.
Apply a simple check for consistency before giving performance feedback.
Plan a meeting format that lets people contribute in more than one way.
Identify common meeting habits that silence some team members.
lessons.teaching:
Performance feedback is one place where bias can enter everyday supervision. Vague comments such as needs more presence, not a culture fit, too quiet, too direct or great attitude are hard to act on and easy to apply unevenly. They tend to reflect how a person's style compares to the supervisor's expectations rather than the work itself. The same assertive email can be read as confident from one person and abrasive from another. Specific feedback protects everyone: it tells the person exactly what happened, why it matters for the work and what to do next.

A simple method helps. Describe the situation, the observable behavior and its effect on the work, then agree on the next step. For example: In Tuesday's provider call, the timeline you shared left out the county review step, which meant the provider planned for the wrong date. For the next call, please check the timeline against the review checklist. Before giving feedback, ask yourself two questions. Would I say the same thing, in the same words, to another team member who did the same thing? Does this concern a specific job requirement or merely my preference for how someone talks, dresses or socializes? If a style concern affects the work, identify the observable effect and consult HR about any accommodation, religious practice or protected characteristic before imposing a requirement. Keep brief notes throughout the year so reviews rest on a record, not on the most recent or most memorable moment.

Meetings are the other daily test. Common habits favor people who think aloud and speak first: open discussion with no agenda, decisions made in the last few minutes, side conversations in the room while remote participants wait, and interruptions that go unaddressed. Inclusive meetings are designed, not hoped for. Send an agenda and materials in advance. Say what decision is needed. Offer a round with the option to pass, and invite written input through an accessible channel. Set a realistic input deadline before the decision; if later comments arrive, explain whether and how they can still affect it. Make sure remote participants and people using captions or interpreters can follow and join. Credit ideas to the person who first raised them. Rotate note taking and facilitation.

None of this means lowering standards. Consistent job-related standards, effective accommodations and more than one way to contribute help supervisors assess the full range of their team’s work. Consistency does not require identical arrangements for every employee.
lessons.keyPoint: Tie feedback to observable work and its effects, check that you would say the same thing to anyone, and design meetings so contribution does not depend on speaking first.
lessons.example: Practice case: Marcus is drafting a mid-year review for Thao, a program consultant. His draft says Thao is quiet in meetings and should show more leadership presence. When Marcus looks at his notes, he sees that Thao's written analysis shaped two policy decisions and that Thao often sends ideas by email after meetings. The unit's meetings are open discussions without agendas, and two senior staff usually speak first.
lessons.question: What should Marcus do next?
choices: Keep the comment, since leaders need to speak up and Thao will need to adapt.
Remove the comment and avoid mentioning meetings at all to keep the review positive.
Rewrite the review around Thao's documented work, discuss any specific meeting goal with examples, and change the meeting format so written input counts.
feedback: Presence is vague and is not tied to a work result. Keeping it rewards one style and ignores Thao's documented contributions.
Avoiding the topic removes a vague comment but leaves Thao without useful feedback and leaves the meeting format unchanged.
This is the strongest response. It bases the review on evidence, keeps any development goal specific and fixes the meeting design that made Thao's input less visible.
lessons.reflection: Think of a piece of feedback you once received that was hard to act on. What would have made it useful? Have you given similar feedback yourself?
lessons.action: Before your next team meeting, share the agenda and decision needed. Offer a round with the option to pass and a written input route with a clear deadline before the decision. Review whether the format brought forward relevant ideas that the previous approach missed.

check.question: Which piece of feedback is most specific and work based?
check.correct: Your summary of the county contract left out the two open compliance items, so the director approved it without them. Next time, check the summary against the open-items list.
wrong: You need to be more of a team player and show more energy in meetings.
You have a great attitude, but people sometimes find your style a bit much.
check.feedback: Useful feedback names the situation, the behavior and the effect on the work, then a next step. Comments about energy, attitude or style are vague and easy to apply unevenly across different people.

lessons.title: Handling concerns, formal routes and labor agreements
objectives: Explain the difference between concerns a supervisor can resolve and those that must go to a formal office.
Identify the Equal Opportunity and Access Division, Human Resources, labor relations and the ADA coordinator as formal routes.
Describe what retaliation is and how supervisors prevent it.
Locate and apply the relevant collective bargaining agreement before acting on a work rule or discipline question.
lessons.teaching:
Team members will bring you concerns: a heavy workload, a conflict with a coworker, a comment that felt demeaning, a schedule problem, a question about pay. Many everyday concerns are yours to address. You can clarify priorities, adjust assignments, set expectations for respectful conduct and follow up. Some concerns are not yours to resolve alone. Under HR/LR Policy 1436, managers and supervisors must immediately report allegations or incidents of protected-class harassment or discrimination to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow agency complaint procedures. At DHS, involve Equal Opportunity and Access through the designated reporting route. Do not wait to establish whether the allegation is proven. Report related retaliation concerns through the responsible process as well. Accommodation questions go to Human Resources or the ADA coordinator. Questions about discipline, grievances, leave and contract terms go to Human Resources and labor relations. When in doubt, consult before acting.

When someone raises a serious concern, listen and make a factual record in an approved secure location. Explain the required referral and limits on confidentiality; do not promise a particular outcome. Address immediate safety needs through the appropriate emergency or agency response process without waiting for a routine consultation. Do not investigate on your own, question witnesses or confront the person accused before talking with Human Resources or the Equal Opportunity and Access Division. Protect the person who raised the concern. The EEOC explains that complaining about discrimination, taking part in an investigation or requesting a disability or religious accommodation is protected activity. Retaliation can include a poor review, a less desirable assignment, closer scrutiny, exclusion or a changed schedule that makes life harder. These actions can be retaliatory when motivated by protected activity; an unfavorable decision is not automatically retaliation. Keep decisions tied to documented, lawful work reasons and consult HR about timing and effects. Protected activity does not remove legitimate performance expectations, but it must never become a reason for worse treatment.

Many DHS employees are covered by collective bargaining agreements, such as the contracts negotiated with AFSCME and the Minnesota Association of Professional Employees, and supervisors also work under plans for employees who are not represented. Minnesota Management and Budget publishes these agreements. They set rules on matters such as hours, overtime, seniority, vacancies, discipline and grievance steps, and they may give employees the right to union representation in certain meetings. Read the article that applies before changing a schedule, handling a vacancy or starting any discipline. Many problems for new supervisors come from well-meant decisions made without checking the contract. Labor relations staff and your Human Resources partner can explain how the contract applies.

Administrative Procedure 21 requires the applicable Supervisor Core training during probation for classified supervisors before permanent certification. Unclassified supervisors are encouraged to attend; check any additional agency requirement with HR. This optional course does not replace required training. Your job is not to be the expert on every rule. It is to recognize when a formal process applies, bring in the right partner quickly and treat people fairly while it works.
lessons.keyPoint: Resolve everyday concerns yourself, but route discrimination, harassment, retaliation, accommodation, discipline and contract questions to the responsible office, and never let a concern count against the person who raised it.
lessons.example: Practice case: Fatuma, a case aide, tells her supervisor, Eric, that a senior coworker, Greg, has twice mocked her accent in team chat and once in a meeting. She asks Eric not to make a big deal of it because she does not want trouble. Eric is new and worried that reporting it will damage the team. He is also planning to change the team's phone coverage schedule next week, which would move Fatuma to the late shift.
lessons.question: What should Eric do next?
choices: Talk to Greg informally, tell him to cut it out, and keep the schedule change as planned.

Thank Fatuma, explain that he must consult the Equal Opportunity and Access Division and Human Resources, and pause the schedule change until he confirms it is work based and consistent with the contract.
Respect Fatuma's wish and take no action unless it happens again.
feedback: A private warning may seem kind, but it skips the required route, and moving Fatuma to a worse shift right after her report could look like retaliation.

This is the strongest response. Eric must immediately report the possible protected-class harassment through the required route, without waiting for proof. He should promptly review the proposed shift change with HR for legitimate reasons, contract compliance and retaliation risk, while maintaining necessary service coverage.
Comments about someone's accent may involve national origin. A supervisor who learns of possible harassment has a duty to act through the formal route, even if the employee is hesitant.
lessons.reflection: What makes it hard for you to bring in a formal office when someone raises a concern? What would help you do it sooner?
lessons.action: Locate the collective bargaining agreement or compensation plan that covers each of your direct reports, bookmark the articles on hours, vacancies and discipline, and save the contacts for your Human Resources partner, labor relations and the Equal Opportunity and Access Division.

check.question: Which of these is protected activity under federal equal employment law, as the EEOC describes it?
check.correct: Requesting an accommodation for a disability or a religious practice.
wrong: Declining a stretch assignment that the employee does not want.
Disagreeing with a supervisor about a project deadline.
check.feedback: Requests for disability or religious accommodation are protected activity. Ordinary disagreements or declined assignments are not automatically protected on the facts given; they can become part of protected activity when tied to a discrimination concern or another legal protection. Consult HR about the actual context.

cards.back: A simple running record of significant and routine tasks and who received them, used to spot and correct uneven distribution of opportunity and invisible work.
Any statement that an employee needs a change at work for a medical reason. No legal words are needed; supervisors respond and route it to Human Resources or the ADA coordinator.
Feedback that names the situation, the observable behavior, its effect on the work and a next step, rather than personality or style.
Actions such as reporting discrimination, taking part in an investigation or requesting an accommodation. Treating someone worse because of them is retaliation.
The contract between the state and a union that sets rules on hours, vacancies, discipline, grievances and more. Check it before acting.

aid.heading: Every week
items: Hold each one-to-one as scheduled, with the employee's items first.
Update the assignment log and check who received visible and invisible work.
Recognize specific contributions and credit ideas to the person who raised them.
Send meeting agendas in advance and offer a written way to contribute.

aid.heading: When someone asks for a change for a medical or religious reason
items: Treat plain-language statements as possible requests.
Ask what would help; do not ask for a diagnosis or records.
Document the request and contact Human Resources or the ADA coordinator promptly.
Keep the reason private and follow up with the employee on timing.

aid.heading: When someone raises a concern
items: Listen, take notes and explain what happens next without promising secrecy.
Immediately report protected-class harassment or discrimination through the required HR or Affirmative Action route; involve DHS Equal Opportunity and Access and report related retaliation concerns.
Promptly review potentially adverse decisions with HR for lawful work reasons, retaliation risk and service continuity; do not freeze every routine decision solely because a concern was raised.
Check the labor agreement and consult labor relations before any discipline or schedule change.

sources.note: Plain-language requests, the interactive process, limits on medical documentation and the employer's choice among effective accommodations. Formal determinations belong to the agency accommodation process.

sources.note: Executive branch policy on how requests are made, what supervisors may approve, consultation with the agency ADA coordinator before any denial, confidentiality and status updates. Check the current DHS procedure for local steps.

sources.title: U.S. EEOC — Retaliation
sources.note: Defines protected activity, including requesting a disability or religious accommodation, and gives examples of retaliation.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Administrative Procedure 21
sources.note: Classified supervisors must complete applicable core training during probation before permanent certification. Unclassified managers and supervisors are encouraged, not required by this procedure, to complete it.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Labor Contracts and Pay Plans
sources.note: Official source for state collective bargaining agreements and compensation plans. Labor relations and Human Resources interpret how they apply.

sources.title: Harvard Business Review — Bourke and Titus, Why Inclusive Leaders Are Good for Organizations, and How to Become One (2019)
sources.note: Consulting research drawing on about 3,500 employee ratings of 450 leaders; identifies six inclusive leader behaviors and finds leaders often overestimate their inclusiveness. Not a controlled study.

sources.note: Managers and supervisors must immediately report protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer, and follow agency complaint procedures.
